title: The pseudouridine synthase PUSL1 modifies U39 of mitochondrial tRNAs and is linked to human neurological phenotypes.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and parsed both copies of the processed table: GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus) GSE281373_mitochondria_psi_profiling.xlsx (186 KB) and Supplementary Data 1 from the article's supplement (146 KB). Both are 454 data rows x 40 columns, one row per 'tRNA:position' (e.g. MT_TF:39), covering 22 human mitochondrial transfer RNAs at positions 1-77; no duplicate row IDs and no missing values. Columns are truncated reads, coverage, and stopRatio (reverse-transcription stop ratio, 0-1) for 12 samples (4 knockout, 4 overexpression, 4 wild-type) plus three p-value columns. Only 9 rows are at position 39, the site the paper is about; 43 rows have WT-vs-knockout p < 0.05. I also read the two supplementary Word files (figure legends and patient clinical descriptions) and confirmed the GEO series has 12 samples, CC-BY licence.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: That the stopRatio is computed by dividing reads stopping one nucleotide downstream of the modified site by coverage at that position, and that significance came from a generalized linear mixed-effects model in R (lme4). The raw sequencing reads themselves were not downloaded (policy: no fastq). Patient-derived primer-extension results are gel images only, not tabulated.

a1_downloadable.note: Both the GEO processed Excel file and the article supplement downloaded without login; article is Creative Commons Attribution (CC-BY).

a2_label_is_a_column.note: stopRatio (pseudouridine level per position) is already a column in the file, with per-sample values and p-values.

a3_inputs_present.note: Only the tRNA name and position are given, not the sequence; but these are 22 human mitochondrial tRNAs, so sequence lookup is trivial, not thousands of lookups.

a4_units_stated.note: stopRatio is a dimensionless 0-1 ratio of truncated reads to coverage, defined in the methods; truncated and coverage are read counts. README sheet defines KO/OE/WT.

a5_enough_rows.note: 454 labelled positions total, from 22 mitochondrial tRNAs in one human cell line. Only 9 rows are the position-39 sites the paper identifies, and only 43 of 454 reach p<0.05 for knockout-vs-wild-type. Far under the ~1,500-row bar, and the 22 tRNAs are the real independent unit.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially small; verified by downloading both files.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The GEO copy and the supplement copy have the same 454 site IDs and identical truncated-read counts, but different denominators ('full' vs 'coverage', mean difference ~92 reads) and therefore different stopRatio values (mean absolute difference ~0.010-0.013, maximum ~0.36-0.41). Same measurement, two deposited values, no way to tell which is right. Also, in both files the 12 wild-type columns are mislabelled 'OE1-OE4' in the sub-header row.

a8_label_provenance.note: stopRatio comes from a physical chemical-probing measurement (CMC adduct causing reverse-transcription stops), not from another model's predictions.

existing_models.name: iPseU-CNN (convolutional neural network for pseudouridine sites)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported on the standard H_990/S_628/M_944 benchmark sets with independent test sets; accuracies in the high 80s percent (from search result abstracts, not re-run by me)
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Generalization beyond the small curated benchmark sets

existing_models.name: Porpoise (stacked ensemble pseudouridine site predictor)
existing_models.score_and_split: Benchmarked across human, yeast and mouse datasets with 18 sequence encodings and 9 algorithms (from abstract)
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Cross-species transfer and dependence on sequence encoding choice

existing_models.name: PseUdeep / MU-PseUDeep / Definer / PseU-ST / Meta-PseU (deep-learning pseudouridine site predictors, 2020-2026)
existing_models.score_and_split: PseU-ST reports 93.6%/87.7%/89.6% accuracy on H_990, S_628, M_944 (from abstract); Meta-PseU stacks 32 classifiers aimed at generalizability
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Generalizability across datasets; short-sequence bias of the classic benchmarks

existing_models.name: PULSE (PseudoUridyLation Site Estimator, convolutional network on Psi-seq profiling data)
existing_models.score_and_split: Trained on pseudouridine profiling data to characterize sequence features (from abstract)
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Sequence context alone explains only part of site selection

backbone.name: RNA-FM (RNA language model) would be the natural backbone for pseudouridine context prediction
backbone.licence: Open, but irrelevant here because the dataset is too small to train or honestly evaluate a head

integration.partner_dataset: RMBase / MODOMICS (catalogues of RNA modification sites) could supply many more pseudouridine sites
integration.join_key: transcript name + position (and genomic coordinate on the human mitochondrial genome, rCRS build)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Which uridines in an RNA get pseudouridylated and by which enzyme — but answering it needs the large catalogues, not these 454 mitochondrial tRNA positions, so this paper's table would only ever be a 9-site test case.

controls.positive_control: The 9 position-39 sites must come out as the strongest knockout-sensitive positions; they do in the file (p-values rounded to 0).
controls.negative_control: Shuffling sample labels within position, or comparing PUS1-knockout positions.
controls.external_validation: Earlier mitochondrial pseudouridine maps (e.g. RPUSD3/RPUSD4 studies) overlap only a handful of sites.

honest_claim_h3: Any model built on this file could only claim something about 454 uridine positions in 22 human mitochondrial transfer RNAs measured in one HEK-293T cell line, which is too narrow to be a prediction task rather than a description of the experiment.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use RNA sequence context to predict which uridines carry the chemical mark pseudouridine in mitochondrial transfer RNAs.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example would be one uridine position in a mitochondrial transfer RNA with its surrounding sequence and predicted fold; there are 454 such positions across 22 tRNAs, which I verified in the file.
plain_idea.predict: The pseudouridine level at that position, measured as the reverse-transcription stop ratio in CMC-treated RNA sequencing (a chemical probing assay), and how much it drops when the PUSL1 enzyme is knocked out.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Groups studying RNA modification enzymes would like to know which uridines a given enzyme picks, but this dataset is far too small to answer that, so the realistic value is as a 9-site sanity check on models trained elsewhere.

more_or_better_data.why: 454 positions from one cell line versus the standard benchmark sets used by the published predictors (H_990, S_628, M_944) and the much larger RMBase catalogues; ours is smaller by one to three orders of magnitude.

confidence_score.why: Four biological replicates per condition do let you estimate measurement noise, which the sequence-based predictors do not report, but with 9 positive sites there is nothing to calibrate.

models_beatable.why: Several predictors date from 2019-2022 with small benchmark sets and random splits, so they are in principle beatable, but a 2026 meta-classifier (Meta-PseU) explicitly targets generalizability, and we have no data to beat them with.

guaranteed_improvement.why: The condition that fails is sample size: our 454 positions cannot be added to their training sets in a way that changes their predictions, and the assay (CMC reverse-transcription stops in mitochondria) differs from the assays behind their benchmark labels.

ml_idea: The only coherent task would be predicting per-position pseudouridine level (reverse-transcription stop ratio) from mitochondrial transfer RNA sequence and structure context, with knockout-versus-wild-type change as a second target. It dies on size: 454 positions, 9 of them the sites of interest, 22 tRNAs from a single human cell line.

effort.compute_note: Estimated from the actual file sizes I downloaded (0.4 MB total, 454 rows); everything here runs in seconds on a laptop, which is exactly the problem.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the rows and the positives in the deposited table: 454 positions, 9 at position 39, 43 significant at p<0.05 — done in five minutes and it kills the project.

verdict_reason: Fails A5 on size: 454 labelled positions across 22 mitochondrial transfer RNAs from a single human cell line, with only 9 sites at the position the paper is about and 43 significant sites in total — orders of magnitude short of a trainable set, and the real independent unit is the 22 tRNAs. It also fails A7: the GEO deposit and the article supplement give different coverage denominators and therefore different stopRatio values for the same 454 sites (mean absolute difference ~0.01, maximum ~0.4), with no way to tell which is correct, and both files mislabel the wild-type columns as overexpression. Separately, sequence-based pseudouridine site prediction is a crowded field with at least six open models (iPseU-CNN, Porpoise, PseUdeep, MU-PseUDeep, Definer, PseU-ST, Meta-PseU), so even the widened version of the project has no edge. The paper is a clean piece of molecular biology; it is just not a machine-learning dataset.
